 Egypt targets LE 15,000 minimum wage for state employees by 2030
 BY
 Egypt Today staff
 -
 Sat, 24 Oct 2026 - 03:47 GMT
 BY
 Egypt Today staff
 Sat, 24 Oct 2026 - 03:47 GMT
 CAIRO – 24 October 2026: Egypt aims to raise the minimum monthly wage for state employees to LE 15,000 by the end of fiscal year 2029/2030, up from LE 8,000 currently, Prime Minister Mostafa Madbouly announced on Saturday. 
 The proposed increase of LE 7,000, equivalent to 87.5 percent, is expected to cover around 4.5 million employees in the state’s administrative apparatus. 
 Madbouly announced the target during the closing session of Egypt Forum 2026 in the New Capital, saying it was among the recommendations adopted following the forum. He did not provide a detailed timetable for the planned increases or explain how they would be implemented. 
 The announcement comes as households continue to face pressure from rising living costs, while higher global energy prices and the depreciation of the Egyptian pound have increased import costs and added to the burden on the state budget. The US dollar exceeded LE 55 last week. 
 The government raised the minimum monthly wage for state employees to LE 8,000 in July 2026, from LE 7,000 in July 2025. The increase formed part of a package that included a 21% rise in public-sector wage allocations in the state budget. 
 Madbouly also said the government plans to launch a national economic transformation programme in December, covering the following three years. 
 The announcement comes as Egypt approaches the end of its current $8 billion financing programme with the International Monetary Fund (IMF) at the end of 2026. The government has indicated that it does not intend to seek a new financing agreement. 
 Egypt unveiled the initial framework of its National Economic Transformation Programme for 2027–2030 on Friday. The programme focuses on economic stability, private-sector participation and improving quality of life. 
 It targets economic growth of 6.8% by fiscal year 2029/2030, while aiming to reduce inflation to 7% and unemployment to 5.5%. Agriculture, industry, communications and information technology, tourism and energy have been identified as priority sectors. 
 Egypt is preparing for the eighth and final review of its current IMF programme, which could pave the way for the release of a remaining tranche worth around $1.5 billion, subject to approval by the fund’s Executive Board. 
 Egypt also faces additional fiscal pressure from rising global oil prices. President Abdel Fattah El-Sisi said during the forum on Thursday that the financial burden resulting from higher petroleum prices exceeds the country’s capacity to bear it, given the limited resources available to meet energy needs. 
 Madbouly said the state budget had been prepared on the assumption of an oil price of $75 per barrel, while prices had risen to around $110, increasing the cost of securing the country’s fuel and natural gas requirements. 
 Egypt’s fiscal year begins on July 1 and ends on June 30 of the following year.
